extracted.intended_audience: students, philosophers, and scientists interested in the logic of induction and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and guidance for when and how empirical laws, analogical inferences, and causal generalizations may be legitimately extended or relied upon in scientific reasoning; includes when analogy approaches induction and what weakens such inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of derivative (non-causal) empirical laws only to adjacent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative uniformities that are not laws of causation are admissible only where the collocations (conditions of time and place) are known by experience to be such as are requisite for the truth of the law; i.e. only within the conditions of time and place confirmed by actual observation (extensions are to adjacent cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These derivative uniformities are contingent on collocations of causes; if collocations vary the derived uniformities may differ. Example: the succession of day and night on a planet holds only if the same collocation of causes (one sun + rotation) obtains; counteracting or additional causes (second sun, rotation stopped) frustrate the derivative uniformity though not the ultimate causal law. Thus extend empirical derivative laws only to temporally or spatially adjacent cases unless the causal basis is known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of the true causes increases scope and confidence of extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: When we know the causes on which a derivative uniformity depends, we can extend that uniformity farther in time and place, and with less abatement for counteracting causes, than when the law is merely empirical and the causes are unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing causes allows judgment about existence of known counteracting causes and lets us replace local observational bounds by bounds of the ascertained influence of the causes (e.g., day/night applies across the solar system because we know the causal mechanism). When causes are unknown, extension is riskier because unknown counteracting causes might exist elsewhere or later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability of future persistence depends on probabilities of destruction or counteraction of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The warrant for expecting a derivative effect to continue (e.g., 'the sun will rise to-morrow') depends on the probabilities that its underlying causes (sunlight, Earth's rotation) will be destroyed or counteracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed duration without appreciable counteraction as evidence: if causes have persisted for millennia with no counteracting cause observed, the chance of abrupt defeat tomorrow is extremely small. But the further into the future one projects, the weaker this warrant becomes because rare or cumulative causes (or new combinations) might manifest over longer timescales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy as resemblance of relations (fundamentum relationis) can be as strong as induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy may be 'resemblance of relations' (fundamentum relationis) — e.g., colonies:mother-country :: children:parents — and when the point of resemblance is the material circumstance on which consequences depend, the analogical argument can amount to a perfect and conclusive induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the circumstance in which two cases resemble each other is shown to be the material circumstance determining the consequences under discussion, analogical reasoning has full force. The key is to establish that the shared relation is the relevant causal or explanatory relation for the inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: General (looser) analogical reasoning pattern and its distinction from induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogical reasoning often takes the form: A and B resemble each other in some respects; a certain proposition m is true of A; therefore m is more likely true of B. It differs from a complete induction because no invariable conjunction between the known properties and m has been previously established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogical inference is probabilistic: it assumes that m depends on some property of A (unknown which) and that B shares one or more of the remaining candidate properties. Unlike induction, analogy lacks demonstrated invariant connections; use it when methods of agreement/difference can't be applied but recognize the inference is weaker than a complete induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use properties known to be unconnected with the target attribute
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties employed in an analogy must not be properties that are known (by elimination or deduction) to be unconnected with the attribute m being inferred; if they are known to be irrelevant, the analogical argument is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before drawing an analogical inference, eliminate properties known to be immaterial. The remaining shared properties are the only legitimate basis for probabilistic inference. Anti-pattern: reasoning from superficial or demonstrably irrelevant similarities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every proved resemblance increases probability; resemblance in ultimate properties is strongest
rubrics_metrics.description: Every resemblance between A and B that is not known to be immaterial affords some degree of probability that B has m; resemblance in an ultimate property implies resemblance in all derivative properties depending on it and thus gives the strongest assurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the shared resemblance is an ultimate property, inference of derivative properties approaches certainty. If only derivative properties are shared, they provide grounds for expecting resemblance in ultimate properties and hence potentially other derivative properties. Weight resemblances higher the more fundamental they are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissimilarities furnish counter-probabilities and must be weighed against resemblances
rubrics_metrics.description: Every proved dissimilarity between A and B provides counter-evidence against inferring m by analogy; there is a competition between known agreements and known differences which determines the net probabilistic support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the aggregate of known similarities versus known differences; known differences may offset similarities, especially if they concern properties that (empirically or theoretically) bear on m. Example: lunar similarities to Earth may be outweighed by differences (no atmosphere, no water) that are crucial for life, thereby producing presumptions against lunar habitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicting analogies require comparative weighing of analogies and differences
rubrics_metrics.description: A new case may resemble instances where m exists and also resemble instances where m does not exist (conflicting analogies); one must compare the strength and relevance of these competing resemblances/differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve conflicting analogies by examining which analogies hinge on material circumstances relevant to m and which disanalogies are decisive. Examples include artworks resembling different masters in different respects or artifacts showing mixed affinities to cultural styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of analogy depends on extent of known resemblance, known difference, and unknown region
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of an analogical argument depends on (1) the extent of ascertained resemblance, (2) the amount of ascertained difference, and (3) the extent of the unexplored region of unascertained properties; close resemblance, small difference, and extensive knowledge make analogy stronger and may approximate induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative heuristic: if after much observation B agrees with A in 9 out of 10 known properties, one may assign roughly 9:1 probability that B has a given derivative property of A. But keep in mind the proportion of known to unknown properties — large unknown domains weaken analogical weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogical inferences are most useful for adjacent cases in circumstances and as guides to experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogical conclusions are of considerable value primarily when the new case is adjacent in circumstances (not merely time/place) to known cases; even faint analogies are valuable for suggesting experiments or observations that can lead to induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat analogy chiefly as a heuristic: use it to propose targeted experiments (experimenta crucis) or to select promising hypotheses for testing. Do not accept analogical conclusions as final when a complete induction is attainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses that explain many facts and predict others are useful heuristics but not proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis that explains known facts and predicts new ones helps order facts, suggest experiments, and may bear 'great similarity' to the real laws, but should not be accepted as scientific truth merely because it is plausible and fruitful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such hypotheses to guide inquiry and devise tests, but avoid becoming committed to a single prevailing hypothesis; the illusion of truth obstructs discovery by narrowing experimental exploration. Encourage trying all plausible hypotheses that analogical connections suggest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive methods presuppose the universality of causation and this is not established by mere belief
rubrics_metrics.description: All inductive methods (Method of Agreement, Method of Difference, etc.) rest on the assumption that every event has some cause; this universality of causation is assumed rather than proved by those methods, and belief alone is not adequate justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept the universality of causation merely because it is a strong psychological tendency or instinct. 'Belief is not proof' — evidence must appeal to faculties of sense and consciousness and be judged by conformity to fact. Be wary of petitio principii when inductive logic presumes what it seeks to establish.
